questions.explanation:
A BST can be skewed (a chain) with height n [latex]-[/latex] 1. Insertion and deletion may then walk the whole chain.

questions.question: What is the worst case time complexity of inserting n elements into an empty linked list, if the linked list needs to be maintained in sorted order?
questions.explanation:
To keep the list sorted, each insertion must first find its position by walking the list: up to k steps when the list has k elements.

Total in the worst case: [latex]1+2+\cdots+(n-1)=\Theta(n^2)[/latex]

Answer: [latex]\Theta(n^2)[/latex]

questions.question: Let [latex] A [/latex] be an array containing integer values. The distance of [latex] A [/latex] is defined as the minimum number of elements in [latex] A [/latex] that must be replaced with another integer so that the resulting array is sorted in non-decreasing order. The distance of the array [latex] [2,5,3,1,4,2,6] [/latex] is _____
questions.explanation:
Elements we keep must already be in non-decreasing order; all others can be replaced by suitable values. So
distance = [latex]n-[/latex] (length of longest non-decreasing subsequence).

In [2, 5, 3, 1, 4, 2, 6] the longest non-decreasing subsequence is 2, 3, 4, 6 (length 4).

Distance [latex]=7-4=3[/latex] (e.g. [2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 6]).

Answer: 3

questions.question:
Suppose a circular queue of capacity (n-1) elements is implemented with an array of n elements.
Assume that the insertion and deletion operations are carried out using REAR and FRONT as array
index variables, respectively. Initially, REAR = FRONT = 0. The conditions to detect queue full
and queue empty are

options.A:
full: (REAR+1) mod n == FRONT
empty: REAR == FRONT
options.B:
full: (REAR+1) mod n == FRONT
empty: (FRONT+1) mod n == REAR
options.C:
full: REAR == FRONT
empty: (REAR+1) mod n == FRONT
options.D:
full: (FRONT+1) mod n == REAR
empty: REAR == FRONT

questions.explanation:
One slot is always kept empty so that full and empty can be told apart.

- Empty: REAR == FRONT
- Full: the next REAR position would hit FRONT: (REAR + 1) mod n == FRONT

Answer: full: (REAR+1) mod n == FRONT, empty: REAR == FRONT

questions.question:
In a [latex]B^+[/latex] -tree where each node can hold at most four key values, a root to leaf path consists of the following nodes:

[latex] A = (49, 77, 83, -), \, B = (7, 19, 33, 44), \, C = (20*, 22*, 25*, 26*) [/latex]

The *-marked keys signify that these are data entries in a leaf.

Assume that a pointer between keys [latex]k_1[/latex] and [latex]k_2[/latex] points to a subtree containing keys in [latex][k_1, k_2)[/latex], and that when a leaf is created, the smallest key in it is copied up into its parent.

A record with key value 23 is inserted into the [latex]B^+[/latex] -tree.

The smallest key value in the parent of the leaf that contains 25* is __________. (Answer in integer)
questions.explanation:
Leaf [latex]C=(20^*,22^*,25^*,26^*)[/latex] currently covers the key range [latex][19,33)[/latex] (between [latex]B[/latex]'s separators [latex]19[/latex] and [latex]33[/latex]), and is already full (max [latex]4[/latex] keys per node).

Step 1 — leaf split: inserting [latex]23[/latex] gives [latex]5[/latex] keys ([latex]20,22,23,25,26[/latex]), so [latex]C[/latex] splits into [latex]C_1=(20,22,23)[/latex] and [latex]C_2=(25,26)[/latex]. Per the given rule, the new leaf's smallest key, [latex]25[/latex], is copied up into parent [latex]B[/latex].

Step 2 — B overflows too: [latex]B=(7,19,33,44)[/latex] gains the new separator [latex]25[/latex], becoming [latex](7,19,25,33,44)[/latex] — [latex]5[/latex] keys, over the [latex]4[/latex]-key limit. Since [latex]B[/latex] is an internal node, it splits by pushing up (not copying) its middle key, [latex]25[/latex] (the [latex]3[/latex]rd of [latex]5[/latex]), into the grandparent [latex]A[/latex]. This leaves [latex]B[/latex] split into [latex]B_{\text{left}}=(7,19)[/latex] and [latex]B_{\text{right}}=(33,44)[/latex], with child pointers correctly redistributed: [latex]B_{\text{right}}[/latex]'s first child now covers [latex][25,33)[/latex] — exactly leaf [latex]C_2[/latex], the one holding [latex]25^*[/latex].

Step 3 — A absorbs the pushed-up key: [latex]A=(49,77,83,-)[/latex] only had [latex]3[/latex] keys (one empty slot), so it simply accepts [latex]25[/latex] without overflowing: [latex]A=(25,49,77,83)[/latex], no further split needed.

So the leaf containing [latex]25^*[/latex] is [latex]C_2=(25,26)[/latex], whose parent is now [latex]B_{\text{right}}=(33,44)[/latex]. The smallest key in this parent is [latex]33[/latex].

Answer: 33

First, note [latex]\text{bar}(n)[/latex] repeatedly integer-halves [latex]n[/latex] until reaching [latex]1[/latex], counting the number of halvings — this is exactly [latex]\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor[/latex].

[latex]\text{foo}(n)=1+\text{foo}(\text{bar}(n))[/latex] for [latex]n>1[/latex], and [latex]\text{foo}(1)=1[/latex]. So [latex]\text{foo}(n)[/latex] counts [latex]1[/latex] plus the number of times we must apply [latex]\text{bar}[/latex] (i.e. take [latex]\lfloor\log_2\cdot\rfloor[/latex]) starting from [latex]n[/latex] to eventually reach [latex]1[/latex].

Build up the smallest [latex]n[/latex] achieving each target value of [latex]\text{foo}[/latex]:
- [latex]\text{foo}(n)=1[/latex]: smallest [latex]n=1[/latex].
- [latex]\text{foo}(n)=2[/latex]: need [latex]\text{bar}(n)=1[/latex], i.e. [latex]\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor=1[/latex]: smallest [latex]n=2[/latex].
- [latex]\text{foo}(n)=3[/latex]: need [latex]\text{bar}(n)=2[/latex]: smallest [latex]n=2^2=4[/latex].
- [latex]\text{foo}(n)=4[/latex]: need [latex]\text{bar}(n)=4[/latex]: smallest [latex]n=2^4=16[/latex].
- [latex]\text{foo}(n)=5[/latex]: need [latex]\text{bar}(n)=16[/latex]: smallest [latex]n=2^{16}=65536[/latex].

Answer: 65536
